To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
partial lung irradiation (PLI) induces a dose-dependent reduction of pulmonary function and density, and that these changes differ between the irradiated and nonirradiated lung.

the radiation dose to the lung and the dose rate are the most important factors in determining radiation-induced lung injury, and that the dose to the heart and the dose rate also affect the radiation-induced lung injury.
the lung density and the function of the lung are different after partial irradiation of the lung.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effect of partial lung irradiation on the function of the remaining unirradiated lung tissue and on the density of the irradiated lung.
the effects of ionizing radiation on lung parenchymal cells and the consequences of these effects for the development of radiation pneumonitis.
the effects of partial rat lung irradiations on pulmonary function and tissue density.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of radiation on pulmonary function are dependent on the total dose and dose per fraction.

the effects of irradiation on the pulmonary function are not only dependent on the radiation dose and dose rate but also on the irradiation field size, i.e., the volume of the irradiated lung, and the irradiation technique.
the effects of radiation on the lungs depend on the radiation dose and the time after irradiation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of radiation on lung function are complex, with the degree and nature of these effects being influenced by a number of factors including dose, fractionation, volume of lung irradiated and the underlying lung disease.
the results of this research support the hypothesis that the lung is a heterogeneous organ with respect to radiation sensitivity.
we have shown that radiation can cause a significant loss of lung function, but that this effect is highly dependent upon the location within the lungs that is irradiated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the radiation-induced changes in the lung are not uniform across the lung.
there are differences in the response to radiation in different areas of the lung and these differences can be measured using the density of the lungs and their ability to function.
the lung is a complex tissue with a complex microenvironment, and that this complexity is important in understanding the effects of radiation.
